shorts.title: Walt Disney Went Bankrupt Before Mickey Mouse
shorts.description: Walt Disney's first studio went bankrupt. He moved to Hollywood with almost nothing.

scenes.text: Before Mickey Mouse, Walt Disney went bankrupt.
As the story goes, an early boss told him he lacked imagination.
In Kansas City, he started his first animation studio, Laugh-O-Gram. In 1923, it went bankrupt.
He moved to Hollywood with very little money and a suitcase.
In 1928, he released a cartoon with a new character: Mickey Mouse.
Today, Disney is one of the biggest entertainment companies on Earth. Failure isn't the end.

shorts.title: He Bought Starbucks for $3.8 Million
shorts.description: Howard Schultz left Starbucks, started his own coffee shops, then bought Starbucks for $3.8 million.
sources: Wikipedia: Starbucks — 1987 acquisition by Il Giornale

scenes.text: Starbucks used to sell coffee beans, not coffee drinks.
In 1983, an employee named Howard Schultz visited Italy and fell in love with espresso bars.
He wanted Starbucks to sell espresso drinks. The owners weren't interested.
So he left and opened his own coffee shops.
In 1987, he bought Starbucks itself for about three point eight million dollars.
Today there are tens of thousands of Starbucks around the world.

shorts.title: A Milkshake Machine Salesman Took Over McDonald's
shorts.description: Ray Kroc was 52 and selling milkshake mixers when he met the McDonald brothers.
sources: Wikipedia: McDonald's — 1961 buyout of the McDonald brothers

scenes.text: McDonald's wasn't founded by the man who made it famous.
In 1954, Ray Kroc was fifty two and selling milkshake machines.
One restaurant in California ordered eight of them. He had to see why.
It was run by the McDonald brothers, with a super fast kitchen system.
Kroc started franchising it. In 1961, he bought the brothers out for two point seven million dollars.
Today McDonald's is one of the biggest restaurant chains on the planet. The brothers' name stayed. They didn't.

shorts.title: Monopoly's Real Inventor Got $500
shorts.description: Monopoly was based on a game by Lizzie Magie, created to show the dangers of monopolies.

scenes.text: The real inventor of Monopoly got just five hundred dollars.
In 1904, Lizzie Magie patented a board game called The Landlord's Game.
Its goal was to show how monopolies make landlords rich and everyone else poor.
Decades later, a man named Charles Darrow sold a version of it to Parker Brothers as Monopoly.
Darrow became a millionaire. Parker Brothers bought Magie's patent for five hundred dollars.
A game about unfair wealth… with an unfair ending.

shorts.title: Hershey Failed Again and Again Before Chocolate 🍫
shorts.description: Milton Hershey's first candy businesses failed. Caramel saved him, then chocolate made him famous.

scenes.text: The man behind Hershey's chocolate failed again and again.
Milton Hershey started a candy business in Philadelphia. It failed.
He tried again in New York. It failed too.
Back home in Pennsylvania, he started making caramels. This time, it worked.
In 1900, he sold the caramel company for one million dollars and went all in on chocolate.
He built a whole town around his chocolate factory. Hershey, Pennsylvania.

shorts.title: Harry Potter Was Rejected 12 Times 📚
shorts.description: J.K. Rowling's first book was turned down by twelve publishers. An eight-year-old helped change that.
sources: Wikipedia: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone — publication history

scenes.text: Harry Potter was rejected by twelve publishers.
J. K. Rowling was a single mother with very little money when she finished the first book.
Publisher after publisher said no.
Then a small publisher, Bloomsbury, gave the first chapter to the boss's eight year old daughter. She wanted more.
They published it in 1997, with a small advance.
The series has sold over five hundred million copies. Twelve people said no. One kid said yes.

shorts.title: Groupon Said No to $6 Billion From Google
shorts.description: In 2010, Google offered around $6 billion for Groupon. Groupon said no.
sources: Wikipedia: Groupon — rejected Google offer, 2010; IPO 2011

scenes.text: In 2010, Google offered about six billion dollars for a coupon website.
It was Groupon, one of the fastest growing companies in history.
Groupon said no. They thought they'd be worth even more alone.
At first, it looked smart. Its stock market debut in 2011 valued it at over ten billion dollars.
Then growth stalled, copycats appeared, and the stock crashed.
Today Groupon is worth a small fraction of that offer. Would you have sold?

shorts.title: Snapchat Turned Down $3 Billion in Cash
shorts.description: In 2013, Facebook offered $3 billion for Snapchat. Its 23-year-old CEO said no.
sources: Wikipedia: Snap Inc. — 2013 Facebook offer, 2017 IPO

scenes.text: At twenty three, he turned down three billion dollars in cash.
In 2013, Snapchat had no revenue, but millions of teens were using it.
Facebook offered to buy it for three billion dollars.
CEO Evan Spiegel said no. People called him crazy.
In 2017, Snap went public, valued at over twenty billion dollars.
Sometimes saying no is the best deal. Would you have taken the money?

shorts.title: The $400 Juicer You Could Squeeze by Hand
shorts.description: Juicero raised about $120 million. Then reporters squeezed its juice packs by hand.

scenes.text: This startup raised around one hundred and twenty million dollars for a juicer.
It was called Juicero. A Wi-Fi juice press that squeezed special packs of chopped fruit.
It launched at almost seven hundred dollars, then dropped to four hundred.
Then reporters showed you could squeeze the packs with your bare hands, just as fast.
The internet laughed. A few months later, in 2017, Juicero shut down.
Lesson: make sure your product does something your hands can't.

shorts.title: Segway Was Supposed to Change the World
shorts.description: Before launch, Segway was hyped as a revolution. It never came close.

scenes.text: This invention was supposed to change how cities work.
In 2001, before anyone had even seen it, it was one of the most hyped products in tech. Its secret code name was Ginger.
Some famous tech leaders reportedly said it could be as big as the personal computer.
Then it was revealed: the Segway, a self-balancing scooter.
It cost thousands of dollars, and many cities didn't know where to allow it. Sales were far below the hype.
In 2020, the original Segway stopped being made. Hype is not a business plan.

shorts.title: The $75,000 Deal That Made Bill Gates Rich
shorts.description: Microsoft bought an operating system it didn't create, licensed it to IBM, and kept the rights.
sources: Wikipedia: 86-DOS — bought from Seattle Computer Products

scenes.text: The deal that made Bill Gates rich used software he didn't write.
In 1980, IBM needed an operating system for its first personal computer.
Microsoft didn't have one. So it bought one from a small Seattle company for about seventy five thousand dollars.
They adapted it and licensed it to IBM. But here's the genius part: Microsoft kept the rights.
When other companies copied the IBM PC, they all needed that operating system. And Microsoft sold it to all of them.
That's how Microsoft took over the PC world. Read the contract.

shorts.title: Atari Buried Its Failed Game in the Desert
shorts.description: E.T. for the Atari 2600 was rushed out in weeks. Unsold cartridges ended up in a New Mexico landfill.
sources: Wikipedia: Atari video game burial — excavated 2014

scenes.text: Atari buried its failed games in the desert.
In 1982, Atari paid a fortune for the rights to make a video game of E.T.
The game was made in about five weeks to hit Christmas.
Players hated it. Millions of cartridges didn't sell.
In 1983, trucks dumped unsold games in a landfill in New Mexico. For years, people called it a legend.
In 2014, they dug it up. The games were really there. Rushing can cost you everything.

shorts.title: Ben & Jerry's Started With a $5 Course 🍦
shorts.description: Two friends split a $5 ice cream course and opened a shop in an old gas station.
sources: Wikipedia: Ben & Jerry's — founded 1978, acquired by Unilever 2000

scenes.text: Ben and Jerry's started with a five dollar course.
Ben Cohen and Jerry Greenfield were childhood friends who wanted to start a food business.
They split the cost of a five dollar mail order course on making ice cream.
In 1978, with about twelve thousand dollars, they opened a shop in an old gas station in Vermont.
Big chunks, funny names, and free ice cream days made people love them.
In 2000, Unilever bought the company for three hundred and twenty six million dollars.

shorts.title: Canva Was Rejected by Over 100 Investors
shorts.description: Melanie Perkins heard 'no' more than 100 times. Canva is now worth tens of billions.

scenes.text: Investors said no to her more than one hundred times.
Melanie Perkins was a university student in Australia teaching people to use design software.
It was too hard to learn. So she imagined a simple design tool anyone could use online.
She pitched investors again and again. Most rejected her.
She kept going. In 2013, Canva launched.
Today Canva has millions of users and is worth tens of billions of dollars. One yes is enough.

shorts.title: One Line of Text Made Hotmail Worth $400 Million
shorts.description: Every Hotmail email ended with an ad for Hotmail. Microsoft bought it about 18 months after launch.
sources: Wikipedia: Outlook.com — Hotmail history, acquired by Microsoft 1997

scenes.text: One line of text made this startup worth four hundred million dollars.
In 1996, Hotmail launched one of the first free email services you could use from any browser.
At the bottom of every email, they added a line: get your free email at Hotmail.
So every user became an ad. Friends signed up, then their friends.
It grew to millions of users incredibly fast.
In late 1997, Microsoft bought Hotmail for about four hundred million dollars. The best marketing can be free.
